meta.title: Who really said "There Are Things Known, and Things Unknown, and In Between Are the Doors"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Huxley, not Blake, not quite Morrison. Ray Manzarek said a longer version to Newsweek in November 1967, explaining how the Doors got their name.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Are Things Known, and Things Unknown, and In Between Are the Doors'?
meta.ogDescription: Ray Manzarek of the Doors, in Newsweek, 6 November 1967. QI found the line in no text by Huxley or Blake.

answer.label: Not Aldous Huxley — Ray Manzarek said it to Newsweek in 1967
answer.authorDates: 1939–2013 · American keyboardist, co-founder of the Doors
answer.sourceLine: The line derives from Ray Manzarek, the Doors’ keyboardist, quoted in Newsweek on 6 November 1967 explaining the band’s name: ‘There are things you know about, and things you don’t, the known and the unknown, and in between are the doors—that’s us.’ Quote Investigator, which verified that citation on microfilm, has found the polished version in no text by Huxley or Blake, and concludes the quotation should be attributed to Manzarek.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Newsweek, ‘Music: This Way to the Egress’
Ray Manzarek, then 25, co-founder and keyboardist of the Doors

source.excerpt: “There are things you know about,” says 25-year-old Manzarek, whose specialty is playing the organ with one hand and the bass piano with the other, “and things you don’t, the known and the unknown, and in between are the doors–that’s us.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s earliest citation is Newsweek, 6 November 1967, page 101 — located via a 2007 Louisiana State University master’s thesis and then verified on microfilm the 1967 citation ↗.

QI states plainly that it has not located the quotation in the texts of Blake or Huxley. Huxley’s The Doors of Perception (1954) does discuss doors, but the sentence under investigation is not in it what QI checked ↗.

What Blake actually wrote, in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is ‘If the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite’ — the line that gave Huxley his 1954 title, and the band its name at one remove the Blake text ↗.

A 1978 rock encyclopedia claimed the saying appeared on the flyleaf of Huxley’s book and was Blake’s; QI has been unable to find it on any edition’s flyleaf, and found no evidence Blake made the remark. A 1990 advertisement for the film The Doors printed it over Jim Morrison’s name, which is how most people meet it the 1978 and 1990 citations ↗.
source.excerptNote: The familiar version is this sentence streamlined: the conversational ‘things you know about’ tightened to ‘things known’, and the closing ‘that’s us’ — the part that makes it an explanation of a band name rather than a piece of mysticism — dropped entirely. Losing that clause is what let the line pass as Blake or Huxley.

source.rightsHolder: Newsweek (the 1967 article) and the estate of Ray Manzarek (the spoken words)
source.rightsNote: In copyright. The sentence survives because a Newsweek reporter wrote it down in 1967 — long after the 1930 cut-off for the United States public domain — so both the article and Manzarek’s quoted words are protected. Quote it briefly with attribution rather than reproducing the passage. Blake’s ‘doors of perception’ sentence, by contrast, is genuinely public domain; it is simply a different sentence. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Ray Manzarek
author.heading: About Ray Manzarek
author.metaLine: 1939–2013 · American keyboardist, co-founder of the Doors
author.bio: Ray Manzarek co-founded the Doors with Jim Morrison in 1965 after the two met at UCLA film school, and his organ playing is a large part of what the band sounds like. He was also, by a distance, its most articulate explainer — which is why a reporter asking where the name came from got a fully-formed sentence back, and why that sentence outlived the interview and went looking for a poet to belong to.

misattribution.heading: Four names for one sentence
misattribution.intro: The line has been credited to a poet, an essayist and a rock singer — none of whom said it. It belongs to the fourth man, who was explaining a band name to a magazine.

context.heading: Why it sounds like Blake
lead: The name of the band really does come from Blake, by way of Huxley: Blake wrote that if the doors of perception were cleansed everything would appear as it is, infinite, and Huxley borrowed the phrase for his 1954 title. So a sentence explaining that name arrives pre-loaded with two literary ancestors.

Strip off the closing ‘that’s us’ and there is nothing left to mark it as 1967 shop talk. What remains is an aphorism about the known and the unknown — and an aphorism with no visible owner drifts upward, toward the most famous name in reach.
detailsBody: The chain of custody here is unusually legible. A 2007 master’s thesis at Louisiana State University pointed to the Newsweek profile; Quote Investigator followed the footnote and read the article on microfilm. That is the whole provenance — one magazine paragraph from November 1967.

Everything after it is compression. By 1978 a rock encyclopedia was calling the words Blake’s; by 1990 a film advertisement was calling them Morrison’s; by 2010 quotation sites were serving them with Morrison’s dates attached. At no point did anyone add evidence — each step only removed a qualifier.
